title: Five Ways NVIDIA Co-Design Maximizes the Value of Every Byte in the AI Factory | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA argues that with HBM capacity flat at 288 GB per GPU from GB300 to Rubin, AI factory gains now come from raising useful work per byte via five co-designed levers: NVFP4, wide expert parallelism over NVLink, Dynamo KV-cache management, Vera CPU memory offload, and the CMX pod-level storage tier. It claims the combination lets Vera Rubin NVL72 deliver up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 on SemiAnalysis AgentX.

insights.claim: HBM capacity per GPU stayed at 288 GB from GB300 to NVIDIA Rubin while bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s, so generational gains must come from extracting more useful work per byte rather than more bytes.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: HBM capacity stagnation shifts value capture toward software, interconnect and memory-tiering co-design rather than raw HBM content per GPU.
insights.quote: From GB300 to NVIDIA Rubin, capacity held at 288 GB while bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s.

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user on SemiAnalysis AgentX, a benchmark replaying recorded coding-agent sessions with real tool-call gaps.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: A 30x perf-per-watt step for agentic inference, if realized, supports a strong Rubin upgrade cycle in power-constrained data centers.

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames memory waste in AI factories as redundant weight copies, idle-session KV cache and recomputed prefixes, each of which displaces token production in the most expensive memory tier.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Defines the optimization targets where NVIDIA's full-stack approach claims an advantage over component vendors.
insights.quote: The question is no longer how much memory a GPU has, but how much useful work each byte delivers.
insights.locator: In an AI factory, high bandwidth

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues the five levers stack because they form one memory system: a 4-bit KV block saves space simultaneously in HBM, Vera memory and CMX storage.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: System-level co-design is NVIDIA's moat argument against point-solution competitors in accelerators, CPUs and storage.
insights.locator: How do the five levers work together?

insights.claim: NVFP4 uses a 4-bit E2M1 element with an FP8 (E4M3) scale shared by every 16-value micro-block plus a per-tensor FP32 scale, which NVIDIA says preserves accuracy where naive 4-bit formats fail.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Proprietary number formats tied to NVIDIA hardware deepen software lock-in.

insights.claim: Applied to weights, NVFP4 shrinks model footprint about 3.5x versus FP16 and 1.8x versus FP8, freeing HBM for KV cache, larger batches and higher concurrency.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Lower memory per model raises effective capacity per GPU and revenue per accelerator for inference providers.

insights.claim: NVFP4 has become the default precision for open agentic benchmarks with strict accuracy requirements, including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX and MLPerf Endpoints, and delivers up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline at the same interactivity.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Benchmark standardization on an NVIDIA-native format advantages NVIDIA in published comparisons.

insights.claim: NVFP4 KV cache cuts cache footprint by up to 50% versus FP8, keeping about 2x more context on device, and NVIDIA reports it retains over 99% of BF16 baseline scores across 10 DeepSeek-v4-Pro benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Doubling resident context per GPU directly improves long-context agentic serving economics.

insights.claim: Wide expert parallelism in TensorRT-LLM spreads MoE experts over eight or more GPUs; with DeepSeek-R1 at EP64 each GPU holds four experts per layer, 232 of the model's 14,848 expert blocks.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: MoE model serving increasingly requires rack-scale systems, favoring NVL72-class products over 8-GPU servers.

insights.claim: Spreading experts frees HBM for cache, raises GroupGEMM arithmetic intensity through weight reuse across more tokens, and lets the Expert Parallel Load Balancer redistribute hot and cold experts between forward passes.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism by which rack-scale interconnect converts into inference throughput.

insights.claim: GB300 NVL72 delivers 10x the token throughput per megawatt of H200 NVL8 at 100 tokens per second per user, per NVIDIA's figure.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Rapid perf-per-watt obsolescence of Hopper-era fleets affects depreciation assumptions for GPU clouds.

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues wide EP only works because the NVLink scale-up domain absorbs MoE all-to-all traffic; on GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth lets EP32 deliver up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than EP8.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Scale-up interconnect is a key differentiator versus rivals lacking an equivalent rack-scale fabric.
insights.quote: This only works because the scale-up domain makes remote bytes nearly as useful as local ones.

insights.claim: Each Rubin GPU brings up to 288 GB of HBM4 and 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, roughly 20.7 TB of HBM4 per Vera Rubin NVL72 rack.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Quantifies HBM4 content per rack, relevant to memory suppliers' demand models.

insights.claim: NVIDIA Dynamo treats KV cache as a fleet-wide resource through KV-aware routing, disaggregated prefill and decode pools, and a KV Cache Runner that tracks blocks across GPU, pinned CPU and storage tiers using NIXL.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Serving software that controls cache placement extends NVIDIA's value capture into the inference orchestration layer.

insights.claim: Agentic workloads are full of KV-cache reuse opportunities such as system prompts, tool schemas, shared documents and task history, and a request routed to a GPU without its prefix forces a costly re-prefill.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Cache-hit rates become a primary lever on inference cost per token for agent providers.
insights.quote: The bytes existed; they were just in the wrong place.

insights.claim: In separate validation tests, VAST Data showed 35 GB/s to one H100 via GPUDirect Storage and WEKA showed up to 270 GB/s aggregate read throughput across eight H100s through a custom NIXL plugin, indicating external storage need not bottleneck KV-cache supply.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: KV-cache offload opens a new AI-inference demand vector for high-performance storage vendors like VAST and WEKA.

insights.claim: A VAST test using vLLM and LMCache on a DGX H100 showed that loading stored KV cache instead of recomputing it reduced time to first token for Qwen3-32B with a 130K-token prompt.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Supports storage-for-inference as a real latency lever, not just a capacity play.

themes.theme: Vera CPU as warm KV-cache tier

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues a slow CPU costs HBM twice in agentic inference: KV cache sits idle during tool calls, then is often evicted and must be rebuilt by full prefill when the tool returns.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Positions the host CPU as a performance-critical component, supporting NVIDIA's push to displace x86 in AI servers.
insights.quote: A slow CPU therefore costs HBM twice: first as idle residency, then as recomputation.
insights.locator: In a fully subscribed AI factory

insights.claim: The Vera CPU has 88 Olympus cores with 1.8x faster single-threaded performance, 40% lower peak loaded latency than x86 CPUs, and up to 14 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Direct competitive claim against Intel and AMD x86 server CPUs in AI head nodes.

insights.claim: Each Vera CPU provides up to 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X, more than 5x a Rubin GPU's HBM4, connected coherently at 1.8 TB/s over NVLink-C2C, roughly 7x an x16 PCIe Gen 6 link, letting Dynamo park idle-session KV cache during tool calls.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Large LPDDR5X pools per CPU add a meaningful new memory demand line in AI servers.
insights.locator: A fast place to park context

insights.claim: NVIDIA CMX introduces a G3.5 memory tier of Ethernet-attached flash shared at pod level and optimized for KV cache, sitting between node-local SSDs and enterprise storage, which carries replication overhead ephemeral KV cache does not need.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Creates a new storage category NVIDIA defines, potentially compressing margins for traditional enterprise storage in AI inference.

insights.claim: CMX is co-designed across the BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor with an integrated Vera CPU, Spectrum-X Ethernet RDMA, DOCA Memos KV-aware services, and Dynamo/NIXL serving integration.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: NVIDIA extends its content per rack into storage processors and networking.

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims CMX delivers up to 5x higher tokens per second and up to 5x better power efficiency than traditional storage for long-context inference by reusing prefixes across nodes and prestaging context.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: If validated, power-efficiency gains in storage matter for power-capped AI data center buildouts.
